name: High blood pressure
tagline: The silent killer — 1 in 3 SA adults.

urgent.heading: Call 10177 or go straight to hospital if
urgent.primary_message: A hypertensive crisis (BP above 180/120 with symptoms) is an emergency. Don't wait — it can cause a stroke or heart attack.
red_flags: BP reading above 180/120 together with symptoms
Severe headache with vision problems or dizziness
Chest pain or shortness of breath
Sudden weakness, numbness, or confusion (may be a stroke)
Nausea, vomiting, or severe anxiety with high BP
A nosebleed that won't stop together with a high BP reading
Blood in the urine or sudden loss of bladder control

what_is_it.heading: Blood pressure in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries. When that force stays too high for too long, it damages the arteries and the organs they supply — silently, over years.
paragraphs: A normal reading is around 120/80. High blood pressure (hypertension) is generally 140/90 or higher, measured on more than one occasion. The first number is the pressure when the heart beats, the second is the pressure between beats.

Most people with high blood pressure feel completely well. The damage builds quietly in the background — to the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes — until something serious like a stroke or heart attack happens. That is why every adult needs regular checks, even if you feel fine.

items.headline: 1 in 3
items.body: South African adults have high blood pressure. Most do not know.

items.headline: Silent
items.body: Usually no symptoms until damage is done. Only a reading tells you the truth.

items.headline: Treatable
items.body: Free check-ups and free medication at every clinic. Most cases controlled with one daily tablet.

items.headline: Big payoff
items.body: Lowering blood pressure cuts stroke risk by up to 40% and heart attack risk by up to 25%.

pull_quote.text: If you have not had your blood pressure checked in the last year, do it this month. It takes 30 seconds. It can add 10 years to your life.

signs.heading: What you might feel — and what you usually don't
signs.lede: High blood pressure is called the silent killer for a reason. Most people feel completely normal. The only reliable sign is the reading itself.

items.title: Usually — nothing
items.description: Most people with high blood pressure have no symptoms at all. Many find out only when they have a stroke or heart attack.

items.title: When readings are very high
items.description: Severe headaches, blurred vision, chest pain, shortness of breath, or nosebleeds can occur — but only at dangerous levels. These are emergencies.

items.title: Trust the machine, not feelings
items.description: Symptoms cannot tell you your blood pressure. Even people with severe hypertension often feel perfectly fine. Only a reading is the truth.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.myth: If I felt high blood pressure, I would know.
items.fact: You almost certainly would not. Hypertension is silent in most people. The only way to know is to measure.

items.myth: I only need to worry about salt if I add it at the table.
items.fact: Most salt we eat is hidden — in bread, processed meats, soup powders, takeaways, even some cheese. The shaker is a small part.

items.myth: Once my blood pressure is normal, I can stop the tablets.
items.fact: Your blood pressure is normal because of the tablets. Stop them, and it climbs back up. Hypertension is managed, not cured.

items.myth: Blood pressure medication has terrible side effects.
items.fact: Modern medications are well tolerated by most people. If yours causes problems, tell your clinic — there are many alternatives.

prevention.heading: How to keep your numbers down
prevention.lede: Even small lifestyle changes can drop blood pressure by 5–10 points. Most people on treatment can lower their dose with consistent lifestyle work alongside.

items.title: Less salt
items.description: Cook with herbs, lemon, garlic, spices. Read labels — anything over 1.5g salt per 100g is high. Aim for under 5g of salt per day total.

items.title: Move every day
items.description: 30 minutes of brisk walking, 5 days a week, lowers blood pressure measurably within weeks. Free, available everywhere.

items.title: Healthy weight
items.description: Losing even 5 kg can drop blood pressure significantly. Focus on slow, steady changes — not crash diets.

items.title: Check regularly
items.description: Every adult should have blood pressure measured at least yearly — more often if borderline or over 50. Free at every clinic and most pharmacies.

items.title: If you have never been checked, or it has been over a year
items.description: Walk into any government clinic or pharmacy and ask. Two minutes. No appointment. Free.

items.title: If your reading is high once
items.description: Have it checked again over the next 1–2 weeks. A single high reading is not a diagnosis — but it is a reason to confirm.

items.title: If you are diagnosed
items.description: Start medication as prescribed. Take it every day at the same time. Skipping doses lets pressure spike up and down — worse than steady high pressure.

items.title: If you feel fine but have hypertension
items.description: Do not stop your medication. The point of treatment is to feel fine while keeping the numbers safe. Continue exactly as prescribed.

items.title: Track your numbers
items.description: Buy a home cuff if you can (around R400 at most pharmacies). Take a reading once or twice a week. Bring the log to clinic visits.

get_help.heading: Where to start
get_help.lede: Blood pressure care is one of the things South African public clinics do very well. Walk in. No appointment needed.

helplines.name: Find your nearest clinic
helplines.description: Every government clinic offers free blood pressure checks and free first-line medication
helplines.meta: No appointment · no medical aid required · ID helpful

helplines.description: Information, support, and free risk-assessment tools

items.heading: How high blood pressure harms the body
paragraphs: Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against your artery walls. When it stays high for years, that constant extra force slowly stiffens and narrows them.
That is why untreated high blood pressure quietly raises the risk of stroke, heart attack, kidney damage and vision loss long before you feel anything. The silence is what makes it dangerous.

items.heading: What the two numbers mean
paragraphs: The top number (systolic) is the pressure when your heart beats; the bottom number (diastolic) is the pressure when it rests between beats.
Below 120/80 is healthy. 140/90 or higher on more than one day is high. 180/120 with symptoms is an emergency — go straight to a hospital.

items.heading: Treatment in South Africa
paragraphs: Government clinics give blood-pressure medicine free. Many people need more than one tablet to reach a safe level, which is normal, not a sign of failure.
The medicine works only while you take it. Stopping when you feel fine is the most common reason it climbs back up.
